sentences.text: Titanis was an extinct genus of flightless birds belonging to the order Cariamiformes, a group that includes modern seriemas.
This North American predator looked very similar to the South American phorusrhacids Phorusrhacos and Devincenzia, featuring a preserved premaxilla with a long, sharp beak tip designed for hunting.

It was completely unable to fly, a trait evidenced by the proportional size of its wings and body mass, and is distinguished from other phorusrhacines by the distal end of its tarsometatarsus mid-trochlea being spread out onto its sides.
Recent estimates suggest Titanis stood 1.4 to 2 meters tall and weighed over 300 kg, and the type species of the genus is Titanis walleri.

Titanis is the only known member of the group to have migrated from the South American continent during the Great American Biotic Interchange, making it the sole phorusrhacid known from North America.

Researchers suggested Titanis used its leg strength to break the long bones of medium-sized mammals rather than for high-speed running, though it was estimated to have been able to run at speeds of 65 km/h.

The genus Titanis was described by Brodkorb in 1963 after the first fossils were found by Benjamin Waller and Robert Allen in the Santa Fe River, Florida, and named Titanis walleri during the winter of 1961/1962.
A Titanis fossil was described in 1995 from a pit near Odem, Texas, and Pierce Brodkorb published the scientific description of Titanis in 1983.

Titanis likely preyed on mammals such as Holmesina, Glyptotherium, equids, tapirs, and capybaras, and likely hunted by sight in open, sunlit areas rather than shaded forests, supported by large lacrimal bone expansions that protected its eyes.

Titanis likely used its legs as kicking weapons to access marrow or defend itself, consistent with its large, curved, sideways-compressed claws, and researchers suggested it used its leg strength to break the long bones of medium-sized mammals like saigas or Thomson's gazelles rather than for high-speed running.

Studies found that Titanis and similar large phorusrhacids had a bite force of 133 Newtons at the bill tip and lost significant intracranial immobility, while a 2010 study by Degrange and colleagues used finite element analysis and CT scans to estimate the bite force and stress distribution of the phorusrhacid Andalgalornis.

Titanis is estimated to have been able to run at speeds of 65 km/h, and in 2005, Rudemar Ernesto Blanco and Washington W. Jones examined the tibiotarsus strength of phorusrhacids to estimate speed, though they noted such estimates are unreliable.
Titanis co-existed with large carnivorous borhyaenid mammals for much of its existence and lived alongside placental mammalian predators such as Smilodon, Miracinonyx, Aenocyon, and Arctodus.
The type species of the genus Titanis is Titanis walleri, and Brodkorb grouped Titanis in the subfamily Phorusrhacinae within Phorusrhacidae.
During the Blancan stage, Titanis lived alongside endemic mammals and new immigrants from Asia and South America.

There is a debate regarding the classification of a California fossil, with some studies assigning it to Aiolornis and others to Titanis. Scientist R.M. Chandler suggested that Titanis's wings might have supported a mobile, clawed hand, though this was later disputed. Circumstantial evidence, such as bone fractures, has suggested that Titanis may not have gone extinct until about 15,000 years ago. Research suggests that abiotic environmental factors, rather than competition with carnivores, were the main cause of extinction for Titanis and phorusrhacids.
